LO 1 - Pain Source Differentiation

Clinical sorting

Spinal nerve vs peripheral nerve vs myofascial vs articular lower-extremity pain

Fast exam rule

Lower-extremity complaints become much easier when you first decide whether the story is neuroanatomic, named-nerve, reproducible soft tissue referral, or joint-mechanical. Then your special tests and OMT choices make sense.

EtiologyPain patternPhysical exam cluesClassic lower-extremity examplesOMM implication
Spinal nerve / radicularDermatomal or root-pattern pain; may radiate below knee; paresthesia can follow a root.Myotomal weakness, altered reflex, sensory deficit, positive neurodynamic test such as straight-leg raise or femoral stretch; lumbar motion may reproduce symptoms.L4-S3 irritation causing sciatica; L5 pattern with dorsiflexion weakness can mimic foot drop.Use gentle, indirect, pain-limited OMT. Avoid thrust through unstable, progressive neurologic, infectious, fracture, or cauda equina presentations.
Peripheral nerveNamed nerve territory rather than a spinal dermatome.Tinel/compression at entrapment site; strength loss only in muscles supplied by that nerve; reflexes usually spared unless that nerve carries the reflex arc.Common fibular nerve at fibular head causing foot drop; lateral femoral cutaneous nerve causing meralgia paresthetica; interdigital nerve irritation in Morton neuroma.Treat local somatic dysfunction and entrapment-adjacent tissues, but refer if progressive motor loss or traumatic nerve injury.
MyofascialRegional aching or referral that does not respect a dermatome.TART changes, trigger point reproduces the familiar pain, normal reflexes and neuro screen, pain changes with palpation/stretch/loading.Piriformis referral, hamstring tenderpoints, IT band friction, plantar fascial tension.Counterstrain, Still, BLT, soft tissue, ME, and activity modification are often appropriate after red flags are excluded.
ArticularDeep joint-line pain, groin pain for hip, mechanical catching/locking, or weight-bearing pain.Restricted ROM or painful end-feel, crepitus, effusion, instability, positive joint-specific tests, imaging abnormalities when indicated.Hip/knee OA, labral tear, meniscal tear, ligament sprain, SI joint dysfunction.Balance adjacent mechanics and improve tolerated ROM. Avoid aggressive treatment across acute fracture, dislocation, severe instability, or major tear.

Board-style discriminator

Meralgia paresthetica is sensory-only anterolateral thigh pain from lateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression. If hip flexion, adduction, or quadriceps strength is weak, think beyond meralgia.

Do not miss

Foot drop can be fibular nerve compression at the fibular head, L5 radiculopathy, trauma, cast compression, or central neurologic disease. Motor weakness earns a real neurologic exam.

Q: A patient has burning numbness over the anterolateral thigh, normal reflexes, normal strength, and worse symptoms with pressure at the inguinal ligament. Which pain-source bucket is most likely?

Answer

Peripheral nerve: lateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression, also called meralgia paresthetica.

LO 2 - Gait and Foot Strike
LO 3 - Arches

Biomechanics

Gait phases, foot strike, and the arch system

The lecture frames the foot as a dynamic tripod: weight moves through the heel, the first metatarsal head, and the fourth/fifth metatarsal heads. The arches are not decoration; they are shock absorbers, proprioceptive platforms, and force-transfer springs that influence tibia, knee, hip, pelvis, and axial mechanics.

Gait momentWhat is happeningHigh-yield muscle / fascia ideaWhat dysfunction can look like
Heel strikeInitial contact through the heel; ground-reaction force meets body weight.Tibialis anterior eccentrically controls plantarflexion so the foot does not slap.Foot drop produces toe drag, tripping, or foot-flat contact instead of controlled heel strike.
Foot flatLoading response; the arch lowers to absorb shock.Plantar fascia and intrinsic/extrinsic muscles control pronation and arch descent.Pes planus or navicular/cuboid drop can overload plantar fascia, knee, hip, and pelvis.
Heel offTerminal stance; heel rises as body moves over the forefoot.Gastroc-soleus complex contracts concentrically and tightens the arch for propulsion.Weak push-off, Achilles/gastroc restriction, forefoot pain, or altered stride length.
Pre-swingToe-off/forefoot propulsion before the limb enters swing.Toe flexors and the windlass effect help convert the foot from flexible platform to rigid lever.Hallux valgus, Morton neuroma, transverse arch collapse, or first-ray restriction can reduce propulsion.
Arch / platformMain ideaSomatic dysfunction implications
Medial longitudinal archCalcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms, and first three rays form a spring-like structure.Collapse favors pes planus, plantar fascial strain, tibial internal rotation, genu valgum tendency, pelvic compensation, and lumbar/SI load changes.
Lateral longitudinal archCalcaneus, cuboid, and fourth/fifth rays carry a larger weight-bearing role.Cuboid dysfunction or lateral overload can change ankle stability, knee varus loading, and gait on uneven ground.
Transverse archMaintains metatarsal-head spacing and forefoot shape.Flattening creates calluses and can irritate the interdigital neurovascular bundle, especially between toes 3 and 4 in Morton neuroma.
Rigid high arch / pes cavusLess shock absorption; lateral loading bias.Can hide early collapse because the arch still appears present; often linked with lateral ankle sprain tendency and rigid mechanics up the chain.
OMM lens

When walking is expensive for the patient, look for a treatable foot driver: dropped navicular/cuboid, transverse arch collapse, restricted talocrural dorsiflexion, or plantar fascial tension. Small foot changes can reduce compensatory work at the knee, pelvis, and spine.

Q: During which phase does the gastroc-soleus complex concentrically contract to lift the heel and stiffen the arch for propulsion?

Answer

Heel off. Heel strike is controlled by eccentric tibialis anterior; foot flat is shock absorption; pre-swing is final toe-off propulsion.

LO 4 - Ottawa Rules
LO 5 - Collateral Grading
LO 6 - Terrible Triad

Imaging rules and acute injury grading

Ottawa ankle/knee rules, ankle sprains, collateral injuries, and O'Donoghue triad

RuleGet radiographs when...Exam translation
Ottawa ankle rules - malleolar zoneAnkle pain plus bone tenderness at the posterior edge/tip of the lateral malleolus or medial malleolus, or inability to bear weight for 4 steps immediately and at evaluation.Palpate the distal posterior 6 cm and tip of each malleolus. Do not substitute vague swelling for bony tenderness.
Ottawa foot rules - midfoot zoneMidfoot pain plus bone tenderness at the navicular or base of the fifth metatarsal, or inability to bear weight for 4 steps immediately and at evaluation.Important for inversion injuries with lateral foot pain: palpate base of fifth metatarsal and navicular.
Ottawa knee rulesAcute knee injury with any of: age >= 55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, inability to flex to 90 degrees, or inability to bear weight for 4 steps immediately and at evaluation.Use the rule before deciding the painful knee is "just a sprain." Fibular head tenderness matters.
InjuryGrade / patternExam and imaging appearanceTreatment direction
Ankle sprainGrade I: stretch/slight tear; no functional loss or instability.Mild/moderate pain and swelling; stable joint.Protection, relative rest, early ROM, rehab, and gentle OMT if safe.
Ankle sprainGrade II: incomplete tear, classically ATFL.ATFL tenderness, pain with weight bearing/walking, mild instability, severe swelling.Brace or immobilize as needed, rehab, reassess stability; image if Ottawa positive or unclear.
Ankle sprainGrade III: complete tear, often ATFL plus CFL.Unable to bear weight, mechanical instability, major swelling; may involve multiple lateral ligaments.Refer/imaging. Do not try to "fix" instability with aggressive OMT.
MCL injuryValgus stress injury; often sports/skiing.Grade I stretched/no laxity; Grade II 5-10 mm laxity with firm endpoint; Grade III complete tear/no firm endpoint and laxity in extension. MRI can show edema, high signal, thickening, or discontinuity of MCL.Grades I-II usually conservative. Grade III often surgical consult, especially with ACL/meniscus injury.
LCL injuryVarus stress injury; evaluate posterolateral corner.Grade I stretched/no laxity; Grade II 5-10 mm laxity with endpoint; Grade III complete tear, often with PLC/cruciate injury. MRI is gold standard for grading and associated structures.Grades I-II conservative. Grade III commonly surgical repair.
O'Donoghue / Terrible TriadClassically ACL tear + MCL tear + medial meniscus tear.Lateral trauma to a planted knee; rapid swelling, instability, joint-line pain, possible locking. Some descriptions now note lateral meniscus involvement in variants.Urgent orthopedic/sports medicine evaluation; OMT is supportive only after acute instability and fracture are addressed.

Q: A 22-year-old football player takes a lateral blow to a planted knee and develops instability, effusion, and medial joint-line pain. What is the classic terrible triad?

Answer

ACL rupture, MCL rupture, and medial meniscus tear.

LO 7A - Foot and Ankle Conditions

Common presentations

Pes cavus, pes planus, plantar fascia, bunions, neuroma, foot drop, and ankle sprain

ConditionPresentation / examEtiology or biomechanical driverTreatment and OMM angle
Pes cavusHigh arch, rigid foot, lateral loading, may have pain despite an arch that "looks present."Reduced shock absorption; can be structural or neurologic; may overload lateral foot and ankle.Screen neuro if new/asymmetric; improve mobility where available, support footwear/orthotics, address ankle, fibula, pelvis, and spine compensations.
Pes planusFlat medial arch, weight bearing on navicular, pronation, possible foot/knee/hip pain.Medial arch collapse and plantar fascial strain; can drive tibial internal rotation and genu valgum mechanics.Lift/support arch, treat navicular/cuboid/cuneiform dysfunction, talocrural restrictions, and upstream pelvic/axial compensation.
Plantar fasciitisHeel or plantar foot pain, often worse first steps; possible heel spur; plantar fascial tenderness.Repetitive microtrauma from increased plantar fascial tension; risks include flat arch, weight, pregnancy, poor shoes, repetitive activity.OMT to arch/foot/ankle/calf, stretching, supportive shoes/orthotic support, activity modification, NSAIDs as appropriate.
Hallux valgus / bunionPainful red/inflamed great toe; proximal lateral deviation and distal medial deviation; may cross toes.Altered forefoot loading, tight/high-heel shoes, family history, rheumatoid arthritis; more common in women.Wider toe box, toe spacers, arch support, OMT for first ray/forefoot mechanics, NSAIDs; surgery if refractory/severe.
Morton neuromaDistal foot/toe pain worse with walking or tight shoes; often between toes 3 and 4; Mulder click may reproduce pain.Transverse arch collapse compresses interdigital neurovascular bundle.Lift transverse arch, improve footwear, metatarsal pad/arch support, OMT; steroid injection or surgery if refractory.
Foot dropCatching toes, tripping, weakness of dorsiflexion, dorsal foot/lateral leg sensory symptoms.Common fibular nerve compression at fibular head, cast/bedrail compression, trauma, L5 radiculopathy, or central causes.Neurologic exam and referral when progressive or traumatic; AFO for safety; treat fibular head/peroneal tunnel and lumbar/pelvic contributors when safe.
Ankle sprainMost commonly inversion injury; lateral ankle pain/swelling; assess weight-bearing, malleoli, fifth metatarsal, navicular.Ligament/capsule stretched beyond elastic limit; ATFL most common, CFL with more severe injuries.Use Ottawa rules first. Grade I-II: protection, rehab, OMT after acute fracture/instability excluded. Grade III: refer.

Q: A runner has burning pain between the third and fourth toes, worse in tight shoes, with a click when the forefoot is squeezed. Which condition and arch concept are being tested?

Answer

Morton neuroma from irritation/compression of the interdigital nerve, often linked to transverse arch collapse.

LO 7B - Knee Conditions

Knee patterns

Varus/valgus deformity, meniscus, Baker cyst, ligament injury, IT band, patellofemoral pain, pes anserine, and knee OA

ConditionPresentation / physical examEtiology / image clueTreatment and OMM angle
Varus / valgus knee deformityBow-legged varus or knock-kneed valgus alignment; altered load line through tibial plateau.Foot arch mechanics, developmental alignment, OA compartment loss, or post-traumatic change.Trace force from foot to pelvis. Treat foot/ankle/tibia/fibula/pelvis mechanics and support alignment; image if structural OA or trauma suspected.
Meniscal tearJoint-line pain, swelling, catching/clicking/locking, worse with loaded twisting; medial more common.C-shaped shock absorber tears with weight-bearing twist. MRI can show tear signal reaching articular surface.Conservative if stable; OMT to balance knee mechanics. Locked knee or major mechanical symptoms -> orthopedic referral.
Baker cystPosterior knee fullness/mass, worse with extension, often decreases with flexion.Popliteal synovial cyst from posterior capsule/bursa herniation; US may show fluid collection.Rule out DVT, thrombophlebitis, bursitis, or solid mass. Treat underlying knee inflammation/mechanics; hamstring/popliteal soft tissue can help symptoms.
Knee ligament injuriesInstability after valgus/varus/twist trauma; swelling and pain; stress testing changes endpoint.MCL with valgus stress; LCL with varus stress; ACL/PCL with cruciate tests and MRI signal/discontinuity.Grade I-II often conservative. Grade III or multiligament injury -> refer. Avoid HVLA through unstable acute knees.
Iliotibial band friction syndromeLateral knee pain, often runners/cyclists, worse downhill/stairs; tenderness near lateral femoral epicondyle; Ober may be positive.Repetitive friction/tension from IT band, hip abductor weakness, leg-length or pelvic mechanics.OMT to pelvis/hip/tibia/fibula, soft tissue to TFL/IT band, gluteal strengthening, activity modification.
Patellofemoral pain syndromeDiffuse, poorly localized anterior knee pain; tracking symptoms; tests have limited sensitivity/specificity.Patella not tracking in groove; imaging poorly correlates with pain.BLT patella/tibia, PT for VMO and hip control, rest, bracing/taping. Can progress toward patellofemoral OA.
Pes anserine bursitis / pain syndromeMedial proximal tibial tenderness over sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus insertion; TTP is useful.Bursa inflammation; risks include obesity, deconditioning, high-impact sports, knee mechanical derangement; often found with lateral tibial torsion.Activity modification, OMT/BLT tibia, PT, NSAIDs; steroid injection in refractory cases.
Knee osteoarthritisPersistent joint pain through day, crepitus, ROM loss, no inflammatory morning stiffness pattern.Articular cartilage erosion, irregular joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis/cysts, osteophytes.OMT for tolerated mechanics, weight management, strengthening, PT, meds/injections as appropriate; refer for advanced disease.

Q: Posterior knee fullness that decreases with knee flexion should make you think of what diagnosis, and what dangerous mimic must be considered?

Answer

Baker cyst; consider DVT/thrombophlebitis or a solid mass before treating it as a benign cyst.

LO 7C - Hip Conditions
LO 9 - Hip Pain Differential

Hip by location

Anterior/groin, lateral, and posterior hip pain differentials

Hip pain sorting frame

The deck emphasizes age, location (intra-articular vs extra-articular), and timing (acute, traumatic, insidious). Groin pain usually points anterior/intra-articular; lateral pain points abductors/trochanteric structures; posterior buttock pain overlaps lumbar, SI, piriformis, and myofascial referral.

LocationLikely diagnosesPresentation / examImaging and treatment cues
Anterior / groinHip OA, labral tear, femoroacetabular impingement, flexor/adductor strain, meralgia paresthetica if anterolateral sensory.Hip OA: older patient, gradual pain, antalgic gait, limited flexion and internal rotation. Labral tear: younger/athletic, pain with ROM, click/clunk, positive FABER/FADIR.Hip OA x-ray may show joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, cysts. Labral tear: MR arthrogram. OMT is adjunct after serious pathology excluded.
LateralGreater trochanteric pain syndrome, gluteus medius tendinopathy/tear, trochanteric bursitis, external snapping hip/IT band friction.TTP over greater trochanter, pain lying on that side, stairs, resisted hip abduction, end-range hip rotation, FABER/Ober, Trendelenburg or hip-drop signs.Usually clinical; ultrasound may show gluteal tendon/bursa findings. Treat with OMT, PT, weight loss when relevant, activity change; injection for refractory pain.
Posterior / buttockSciatica/radiculopathy, piriformis syndrome, SI joint dysfunction, hamstring/gluteal myofascial pain, referred hip OA.Clarify whether symptoms are dermatomal, sciatic distribution, cutaneous distribution, or palpation-reproduced referral.Neuro deficits or red flags change management. SI provocation tests and lumbar/hip screen guide next steps.
ConditionKey findingsTreatment direction
Meralgia parestheticaPain/dysesthesia of anterolateral thigh, otherwise normal neuro exam; compression at inguinal ligament; risks include obesity, pregnancy, tight belts, diabetes, alcohol, lead.Remove compression, treat innominate/pelvic mechanics, NSAIDs; rare decompression. Most resolve over months.
Hip osteoarthritisOlder patient, gradual onset, pain with sitting/prolonged standing/ambulation, limited flexion/internal rotation, antalgic gait.PT, OMT for tolerated mobility and surrounding mechanics, analgesia/injections as appropriate; ortho for advanced disease.
Labral tearYounger athletic patient, acute or gradual pain, painful crepitation/clunk, positive FABER/FADIR.MR arthrogram; trial conservative treatment, sports med/orthopedics if persistent mechanical symptoms.
Greater trochanteric pain syndromeLateral hip pain and trochanteric tenderness, pain on side-lying/stairs, gluteal tendon/bursa/IT band component.Balance pelvis/innominate/hip, stretch IT band when appropriate, gluteal strengthening, PT, weight loss, injection if refractory.

Q: A young dancer has groin pain, painful hip ROM, clicking, and positive FABER/FADIR. Which diagnosis and imaging study are most associated?

Answer

Labral tear; best confirmatory study in this lecture is MR arthrogram.

LO 8 - Sciatica

Posterior hip and leg pain

Sciatica definition and differential diagnosis

Definition

Sciatica is pain extending from the low back or buttock along the posterolateral thigh due to irritation of the sciatic nerve or its contributing nerve roots L4-S3. In clinic, patients may use "sciatica" for several different pain generators, so your job is to sort the pattern.

DifferentialClues that support itClues against it / next step
Lumbar radiculopathyDermatomal pain/paresthesia, myotomal weakness, reflex change, positive straight-leg raise/slump; pain may change with lumbar motion.Progressive neurologic deficit, bowel/bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, fever, cancer, trauma -> urgent workup.
Piriformis syndromeGradual buttock pain/tenderness worse with sitting; sciatic nerve irritated near sciatic notch; palpation of piriformis reproduces symptoms.Normal lumbar neuro screen supports extra-spinal source; persistent true neurologic deficit needs further workup.
SI joint dysfunctionButtock/posterior pelvic pain; may follow pregnancy, leg-length discrepancy, scoliosis, enthesopathy, OA, spondyloarthropathy, or somatic dysfunction.Use cluster of provocation tests: FABER, Gaenslen, distraction, thigh thrust, lateral compression, sacral thrust.
Myofascial referralTrigger point or TART changes reproduce familiar pain; referral map is non-dermatomal; neuro exam normal.Treat muscle/fascial driver but keep rechecking if symptoms evolve.
Peripheral/cutaneous nerveNamed nerve territory: lateral femoral cutaneous, common fibular, tarsal tunnel, interdigital nerve.Does not follow L4-S3 root pattern; reflexes generally preserved unless a mixed nerve/reflex arc is involved.
Piriformis syndrome details from lecture

Six described manifestations include trauma to gluteal region, piriformis palpation pain, pain with stooping/lifting sometimes relieved by traction, palpable sausage-shaped piriformis mass, positive Lasegue sign, and mild gluteal atrophy.

Q: Why is "sciatica" not a final diagnosis?

Answer

Because it describes a pain distribution, not the cause. The cause may be L4-S3 radiculopathy, sciatic nerve entrapment, SI referral, peripheral nerve pain, or myofascial referral.

LO 10 - Lower Extremity Screening Exam

Practical exam workflow

Performing the lower-extremity screening exam

The lab emphasized that second-year screening is graded on whether you can gather useful information, name diagnoses, and demonstrate an effect. The sequence below is built from the lab demonstration and keeps the screen organized from observation to recheck.

  1. Observe before touching. Watch gait, stairs, transitions, ADLs, shoe type, shoe wear, and whether the patient favors one leg or carries load asymmetrically.
  2. Standing inspection. Compare arch height, gastroc/Achilles line, patellar position, genu varum/valgum, weight-bearing symmetry, edema, rashes, posture, and leg-length clues.
  3. Supine inspection. Check plantar skin, calluses, warts, coloration, hair growth, pulses, edema, and apparent leg length.
  4. Hip ROM and strength screen. Flexion, extension, internal/external rotation, abduction/adduction bilaterally. Stabilize pelvis/hip for extension so the patient does not roll into false motion.
  5. Knee screen. Flexion/extension, tibial internal/external rotation, screw-home observation, varus/valgus glide, anterior/posterior tibial glide, patellar motion, and effusion/mechanical signs.
  6. Fibular head. Contact fibular head and compare anterior-lateral vs posterior-medial glide; relate findings to ankle sprain, fibular nerve symptoms, and IT band/peroneal tension.
  7. Ankle and foot. Talocrural dorsiflexion/plantarflexion at the talus, subtalar inversion/eversion through calcaneus, forefoot motion, toes, navicular, cuboid, cuneiforms, and metatarsals.
  8. Name, treat, and recheck. State the region, direction of ease/restriction, likely pain generator, and pre/post effect. Rechecking is part of the treatment, not an afterthought.
RegionMinimum screen itemsCommon diagnoses you can name
HipFlex/ext, IR/ER, ab/adduction, gait/Trendelenburg if relevant.Restricted hip IR/ER, flexion loss, abductor dysfunction, femoroacetabular capsule restriction.
Knee/tibiaFlex/ext, tibial IR/ER, varus/valgus, A/P glide, patella.Externally or internally rotated tibia, patellar glide restriction, valgus/varus strain, knee capsule imbalance.
FibulaFibular head anterior-lateral/posterior-medial glide.Anterior or posterior fibular head dysfunction, possible fibular nerve/ankle relationship.
Ankle/footTalus dorsiflexion, calcaneal inversion/eversion, forefoot and individual tarsals/metatarsals.Talocrural restriction, subtalar restriction, dropped cuboid/navicular, cuneiform or ray restriction, arch dysfunction.

Q: During hip extension testing in side-lying, why stabilize the pelvis?

Answer

To avoid mistaking pelvic/lumbar rotation for true hip extension. Stabilization keeps the screen anatomically honest.

LO 11 - OMT Technique Atlas

Lab recipes

BLT, Still, HVLA, and counterstrain for lower extremity dysfunctions

Practical principle

These techniques are not meant to be forced. Diagnose first, place anatomy in a balanced or ease-first setup, add the technique-specific activating force, wait for release or perform the corrective arc, then recheck the exact motion you diagnosed.

TechniqueDiagnosis / setupCore stepsRecheck
BLT tibia / seated kneeSeated patient; screen tibial IR/ER, varus/valgus, A/P tibial glide.Knee between physician knees; compress tibia toward femur; fingers monitor MCL/LCL and tibial plateau; fine tune tibial rotation, varus/valgus, and anterior/posterior glide into balanced ligamentous tension; hold until warmth/softening/expansion/release.Recheck tibial rotation and knee glide; document direction improved.
BLT knee supineUseful when patient cannot sit; physician seated at side of treated knee.Trap ankle between arm/thorax; grasp proximal tibia/fibula; use body lean for compression/distraction; motion-test A/P translation and varus/valgus; ask patient to medially/laterally rotate femur for postural cooperation; hold balance.Compare tibia-femur relationship and symptoms.
BLT patellaAssess patellar superior/inferior, medial/lateral, and clockwise/counterclockwise motion.Lift patella anteriorly to disengage from femur; use patella as handle on knee capsule; stack directions of balance; add dorsiflexion/plantarflexion or knee flex/extension if helpful; hold until release.Recheck patellar glide and tracking-related tenderness.
BLT talocrural/subtalar - Boot JackSupine patient; physician at foot. Diagnose dorsiflexion, talus/calcaneus relationship, inversion/eversion.Grasp calcaneus and neck of talus between thenar eminences; thumbs at malleoli; fingers at posterior calcaneus; apply inferior traction to disengage talus; balance inversion/eversion, flexion/extension, medial/lateral rotation; patient plantarflexes against resistance, then flexes knee/hip 1-2 inches while traction is maintained.Relax knee first, then foot; recheck dorsiflexion/subtalar motion.
Still technique - midfootTargets navicular, cuboid, cuneiforms, or general midfoot restriction.Patient supine; grasp foot with thumbs/thenar on dorsum and fingers plantar; place midfoot bones into collective ease; add compression toward restricted joint; carry through arc toward restrictive barrier; repeat 2-3 times.Motion-test navicular/cuboid/cuneiform and arch response.
BLT hip / femoroacetabular jointSeated figure-4 setup; restricted hip crossed over opposite knee.Physician stabilizes medial crossed femur near hip joint; patient holds crossed knee and slowly circles trunk/hip. Pause or repeat in restricted arcs. Repeat opposite direction. Lecture cue: femur/physician is the bolt; patient is the nut.Recheck hip IR/ER, flexion, and pain.
HVLA tibial rotationDiagnose externally or internally rotated tibia relative to patella.For externally rotated tibia: internally rotate tibia, flex knee to barrier, short J-motion thrust medial-to-lateral. For internally rotated tibia: externally rotate tibia, flex to barrier, short J-motion thrust lateral-to-medial. Avoid if acute instability, fracture, severe sprain, or patient cannot consent/relax.Recheck tibial position relative to patella in flexion and extension.
Counterstrain - lateral hamstringBiceps femoris tender point just below ischial tuberosity or about one-third above distal fibular-head attachment.Patient prone; mark tenderness as 10/10; flex knee markedly, externally rotate tibia on femur, fine-tune hip extension/compression until tenderness <= 3/10; hold 90 seconds; slow passive return.Recheck tender point and knee/hip motion.
Counterstrain - medial hamstringSemimembranosus/semitendinosus tender point within medial hamstring group.Patient prone; flex knee markedly, internally rotate tibia on femur, fine-tune hip extension/compression until tenderness <= 3/10; hold 90 seconds; slow passive return.Recheck tender point.
Technique safety

Acute fracture, dislocation, severe mechanical instability, infection, major neurologic deficit, vascular compromise, or positive imaging-rule red flags shift the plan away from manipulative correction and toward imaging/referral or protective management.

Q: In the bootjack BLT, what patient cooperation follows the physician's traction/balance setup?

Answer

The patient plantarflexes against resistance, then flexes the knee/hip slightly while the physician maintains traction and balance.

LO Integration - Case Vignettes

Putting it together

Case-based integration: choose the bucket, image when indicated, treat when safe

Case 1 - Acute inversion injury

Vignette: Lateral ankle swelling after rolling ankle, cannot take 4 steps, tenderness at posterior lateral malleolus.

Answer: Ottawa ankle positive -> x-ray before OMT. If fracture excluded, grade sprain; Grade III instability gets referral.

Case 2 - "Sciatica"

Vignette: Buttock pain worse with sitting; piriformis palpation reproduces symptoms; neuro screen normal.

Answer: Extra-spinal sciatic irritation/piriformis pattern; treat pelvic/hip/piriformis mechanics and modify provoking activity.

Case 3 - Foot drop

Vignette: Recent cast removal; tripping and weak dorsiflexion; numb dorsum of foot.

Answer: Peripheral common fibular nerve is likely, but compare with L5 radiculopathy. Motor deficit warrants careful neuro exam and follow-up.

Case 4 - Lateral hip pain

Vignette: Middle-aged woman, pain lying on side, TTP at greater trochanter, pain with resisted abduction.

Answer: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome; address gluteal/IT band/pelvic mechanics, PT/strengthening, consider imaging/injection if refractory.

Question stem phraseBest next thought
Cannot bear weight after ankle or knee injuryApply Ottawa rules and image when criteria are met.
Mechanical locking after loaded knee twistMeniscal tear; severe locked knee needs ortho rather than forceful OMT.
Anterior groin pain with positive FADIR/FABER and clunkLabral tear; consider MR arthrogram.
Posterior knee mass that mimics DVTBaker cyst differential; do not delay vascular workup if suspicious.
Diffuse anterior knee pain with poor imaging correlationPatellofemoral pain; treat tracking/VMO/hip mechanics.

Q: What is the safest OMM decision when a patient has acute traumatic knee pain, obvious instability, and inability to bear weight?

Answer

Do not thrust or aggressively mobilize. Use imaging/referral pathways first, protect the joint, and consider gentle supportive OMT only after serious injury is excluded.

Week 5 Lower Extremity - High-Yield One-Pager

Condensed by learning objective: pain-source sorting, gait/arches, Ottawa rules, common conditions, hip/sciatica differential, screening, and OMT.

LO 1

Pain source buckets

  • Spinal/radicular: dermatomal pain, myotomal weakness, reflex change, +SLR/femoral stretch; gentle indirect OMT, avoid thrust if unstable/progressive/cauda equina.
  • Peripheral nerve: named nerve territory (not dermatomal); +Tinel/compression at entrapment site; strength loss only in that nerve's muscles.
  • Myofascial: trigger point/TART reproduces familiar pain, non-dermatomal, neuro exam normal.
  • Articular: joint-line/groin pain, restricted ROM/painful end-feel, crepitus, effusion, instability.
  • Discriminator: meralgia paresthetica is sensory-only anterolateral thigh pain (LFCN) with normal strength/reflex - if hip flexion/adduction/quad strength is weak, think beyond meralgia.
LO 2

Gait & foot strike

  • Heel strike: initial contact; tibialis anterior eccentrically controls plantarflexion so foot doesn't slap.
  • Foot flat: loading response; arch lowers to absorb shock via plantar fascia/intrinsics.
  • Heel off: terminal stance; gastroc-soleus contracts concentrically, tightens arch for propulsion.
  • Pre-swing: toe-off; toe flexors + windlass effect convert foot from flexible platform to rigid lever.
LO 3

Arches

  • Foot tripod = heel + 1st MT head + 4th/5th MT heads.
  • Medial longitudinal: calcaneus-talus-navicular-cuneiforms-rays 1-3; collapse -> pes planus, tibial IR, genu valgum, pelvic/SI/lumbar load.
  • Lateral longitudinal: calcaneus-cuboid-rays 4-5; cuboid dysfunction alters ankle stability/knee varus loading.
  • Transverse: maintains MT-head spacing; flattening irritates interdigital nerve (Morton neuroma, toes 3-4).
  • Pes cavus: rigid high arch, less shock absorption, lateral loading bias, ankle-sprain tendency.
LO 4-5

Ottawa rules

  • Ankle (malleolar): ankle pain + bone tenderness at posterior edge/tip of lateral or medial malleolus, OR unable to bear weight 4 steps.
  • Foot (midfoot): midfoot pain + tenderness at navicular or base of 5th MT, OR unable to bear weight 4 steps.
  • Knee: age >=55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, unable to flex to 90 deg, OR unable to bear weight 4 steps.
LO 4

Ankle sprain grading

  • Grade I: stretch/slight tear, no functional loss/instability -> protect, early ROM, gentle OMT.
  • Grade II: incomplete tear (classically ATFL), mild instability, severe swelling -> brace, rehab, image if Ottawa+.
  • Grade III: complete tear (often ATFL+CFL), unable to bear weight, mechanical instability -> refer/image, no aggressive OMT.
LO 5

Collateral ligament grading (MRI)

  • MCL (valgus stress): Gr I stretched/no laxity; Gr II 5-10mm laxity, firm endpoint; Gr III complete tear, no firm endpoint, laxity in extension. MRI: edema, high signal, thickening, or discontinuity.
  • LCL (varus stress, check posterolateral corner): same Gr I-III pattern; MRI is gold standard for grading + associated structures.
  • Gr I-II usually conservative; Gr III often surgical, especially with ACL/meniscus injury.
LO 6

Terrible triad (O'Donoghue)

  • Classic mechanism: lateral blow to a planted knee.
  • Classic triad = ACL tear + MCL tear + medial meniscus tear (some descriptions note lateral meniscus in variants).
  • Rapid swelling, instability, joint-line pain, possible locking.
  • Urgent ortho/sports med eval; OMT supportive only after instability/fracture addressed.
LO 7 - Common Lower-Extremity Conditions

Presentation, etiology & treatment (foot/ankle -> knee -> hip -> posterior)

ConditionPresentation / examEtiology / driverTreatment / OMM angle

Pes planusFlat medial arch, navicular weight-bearing, pronationMedial arch collapse/plantar fascial strain; drives tibial IR + genu valgumArch support; treat navicular/cuboid/cuneiform + talocrural restriction; treat upstream pelvic/axial compensation
Plantar fasciitisHeel/plantar pain worse first steps; +/- heel spurRepetitive microtrauma from plantar fascial tension; risk: flat arch, weight, pregnancy, poor shoesOMT to arch/foot/ankle/calf, stretching, supportive shoes/orthotic, NSAIDs
Hallux valgus (bunion)Painful red/inflamed great toe; proximal lateral + distal medial deviationAltered forefoot loading, tight/high-heel shoes, family history, RA; more common in womenWider toe box, toe spacers, arch support, OMT first ray/forefoot; surgery if refractory/severe
Morton neuromaDistal foot/toe pain worse walking/tight shoes, usually toes 3-4; +Mulder clickTransverse arch collapse compresses interdigital neurovascular bundleLift transverse arch, better footwear, metatarsal pad/arch support, OMT; steroid injection or surgery if refractory
Foot dropToe catching/tripping, dorsiflexion weakness, dorsal foot/lateral leg sensory symptomsCommon fibular nerve compression at fibular head, cast/bedrail compression, trauma, L5 radiculopathy, or central causesNeurologic exam +/- referral if progressive/traumatic; AFO for safety; treat fibular head/peroneal tunnel + lumbar/pelvic contributors when safe
Ankle sprainMost commonly inversion; lateral ankle pain/swelling; check weight-bearing, malleoli, 5th MT, navicularLigament/capsule overstretched; ATFL most common, +CFL with more severe injuryOttawa rules first; Gr I-II protect/rehab/OMT after fracture excluded; Gr III refer
Varus/valgus deformity (knee)Bow-legged (varus) or knock-kneed (valgus) alignment; altered load through tibial plateauFoot arch mechanics, developmental alignment, OA compartment loss, or post-traumatic changeTrace force foot->pelvis; treat foot/ankle/tibia/fibula/pelvis mechanics; image if structural OA/trauma suspected
Meniscal tearJoint-line pain, swelling, catching/clicking/locking, worse with loaded twist; medial more commonC-shaped shock absorber tears with weight-bearing twist; MRI signal reaching articular surfaceConservative if stable; OMT to balance knee mechanics; locked knee/major mechanical symptoms -> ortho referral
Baker's cystPosterior knee fullness/mass, worse with extension, decreases with flexionPopliteal synovial cyst from posterior capsule/bursa herniation; US may show fluid collectionRule out DVT/thrombophlebitis/bursitis/solid mass first; treat underlying knee inflammation/mechanics
Ligament injuries (knee)Instability after valgus/varus/twist trauma; swelling; stress testing changes endpointMCL with valgus stress; LCL with varus stress; ACL/PCL with cruciate tests/MRI signalGr I-II often conservative; Gr III/multiligament -> refer; avoid HVLA through unstable acute knees
IT band friction syndromeLateral knee pain (runners/cyclists), worse downhill/stairs; tender near lateral femoral epicondyle; +OberRepetitive friction/tension from IT band, hip abductor weakness, leg-length/pelvic mechanicsOMT to pelvis/hip/tibia/fibula, soft tissue to TFL/IT band, gluteal strengthening, activity modification
Meralgia parestheticaSensory-only anterolateral thigh pain/dysesthesia; otherwise normal neuro examLateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression at inguinal ligament; risk: obesity, pregnancy, tight belts, diabetes, alcohol, leadRemove compression, treat innominate/pelvic mechanics, NSAIDs; rare decompression; most resolve over months

Pes anserine bursitisMedial proximal tibial tenderness over sartorius/gracilis/semitendinosus insertionBursa inflammation; risk: obesity, deconditioning, high-impact sports, often with lateral tibial torsionActivity modification, OMT/BLT tibia, PT, NSAIDs; steroid injection in refractory cases
Osteoarthritis (knee & hip)Knee: persistent pain, crepitus, ROM loss, no inflammatory AM-stiffness pattern. Hip: older patient, gradual onset, antalgic gait, limited flexion/IRArticular cartilage erosion, irregular joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis/cysts, osteophytesOMT for tolerated mechanics, weight management, PT, meds/injections as appropriate; refer for advanced disease
Hip pain / GTPSLateral hip pain, TTP over greater trochanter, pain lying on that side/stairs; +resisted abduction, Ober, TrendelenburgGluteus medius tendinopathy/tear, trochanteric bursitis, external snapping hip/IT band frictionOMT, PT, weight loss, activity change; injection for refractory pain
Labral tearYounger/athletic groin pain, painful ROM, click/clunk; +FABER/FADIRFemoroacetabular impingement or traumatic labral injury; MR arthrogram confirmsTrial conservative treatment; sports med/orthopedics if persistent mechanical symptoms
Sciatica & piriformis syndromePain along posterolateral thigh from low back/buttock; piriformis: gradual buttock pain worse sitting, palpable "sausage" mass, +LasegueSciatic nerve/nerve-root (L4-S3) irritation; piriformis compresses nerve near sciatic notchTreat pelvic/piriformis mechanics if extraspinal; urgent workup for neuro deficit/red flags
SI joint dysfunctionButtock/posterior pelvic painPregnancy, leg-length discrepancy, scoliosis, enthesopathy, OA, spondyloarthropathy, or somatic dysfunctionProvocation cluster (FABER, Gaenslen, distraction, thigh thrust, lateral compression, sacral thrust); OMT to pelvis
LO 8

Sciatica & DDx

Definition: pain extending from low back/buttock along posterolateral thigh from irritation of the sciatic nerve or its L4-S3 roots. "Sciatica" is a pain distribution, not a final diagnosis.

  • Lumbar radiculopathy: dermatomal pain, myotomal weakness, reflex change, +SLR/slump.
  • Piriformis syndrome: gradual buttock pain worse sitting, palpation reproduces symptoms, normal lumbar neuro screen.
  • SI joint dysfunction: buttock/pelvic pain, +provocation cluster.
  • Myofascial referral: trigger/TART reproduces pain, non-dermatomal, neuro normal.
  • Peripheral/cutaneous nerve: LFCN, common fibular, tarsal tunnel, interdigital - doesn't follow root pattern.
  • Piriformis 6 signs: gluteal trauma hx, piriformis palpation pain, pain w/ stooping/lifting relieved by traction, palpable "sausage" mass, +Lasegue, mild gluteal atrophy.
LO 9

Hip pain by location

  • Anterior/groin: hip OA (older, gradual, antalgic gait, limited flex/IR), labral tear (younger/athletic, click/clunk, +FABER/FADIR, MR arthrogram), FAI, flexor/adductor strain, meralgia if sensory-only.
  • Lateral: GTPS, gluteus medius tendinopathy/tear, trochanteric bursitis, external snapping hip/IT band friction; TTP trochanter, pain side-lying/stairs, +Ober/Trendelenburg.
  • Posterior/buttock: sciatica/radiculopathy, piriformis syndrome, SI dysfunction, hamstring/gluteal myofascial, referred hip OA; clarify dermatomal vs sciatic vs cutaneous vs palpation-reproduced pattern.
LO 10

Screening exam sequence

  • Observe gait, stairs, transitions, shoe type/wear, load asymmetry.
  • Standing: arch height, gastroc/Achilles line, patellar position, genu varum/valgum, LLD clues.
  • Supine: plantar skin, pulses, edema, apparent leg length.
  • Hip ROM/strength (stabilize pelvis in extension); knee flex/ext, tibial IR/ER, varus/valgus, A/P glide, patella.
  • Fibular head glide; talocrural dorsi/plantarflexion, subtalar inv/ev, forefoot/tarsals.
  • Name region + direction of ease/restriction + likely generator; treat; recheck (recheck is part of treatment).

RegionMinimum screen itemsCommon diagnoses you can name

Knee/tibiaFlex/ext, tibial IR/ER, varus/valgus, A/P glide, patellaExternally/internally rotated tibia, patellar glide restriction, valgus/varus strain, knee capsule imbalance

LO 11 - OMT Technique Atlas

BLT, Still, HVLA & counterstrain by region

RegionTechniqueKey setup / recipe
Knee - seatedBLTKnee between physician's knees; compress tibia toward femur; fingers monitor MCL/LCL/tibial plateau; fine-tune tibial rotation, varus/valgus, A/P glide into balanced ligamentous tension; hold until release; recheck rotation/glide
Knee - supineBLTPhysician seated at side; trap ankle between arm/thorax; grasp proximal tibia/fibula; lean for compression/distraction; motion-test A/P + varus/valgus; patient rotates femur to cooperate; hold balance
PatellaBLTAssess superior/inferior, medial/lateral, CW/CCW motion; lift patella anteriorly off femur, use as handle on capsule; stack directions of balance; add ankle/knee flex-ext if helpful; hold until release
Hip (femoroacetabular)BLTSeated figure-4 (restricted hip crossed over opposite knee); physician stabilizes femur near hip joint ("bolt"); patient ("nut") slowly circles trunk/hip, pausing/repeating in restricted arcs; repeat opposite direction; recheck IR/ER, flexion, pain
Talocrural/subtalar (Boot Jack)BLTSupine; grasp calcaneus/talar neck between thenar eminences, thumbs at malleoli, fingers posterior calcaneus; inferior traction disengages talus; balance inversion/eversion, flex/ext, rotation; patient plantarflexes against resistance then flexes knee/hip 1-2 inches while traction held; relax knee first, then foot
Midfoot (navicular/cuboid/cuneiforms)StillSupine; thumbs/thenar on dorsum, fingers plantar; place midfoot bones into collective ease; add compression toward restricted joint; carry through arc toward restrictive barrier; repeat 2-3 times; motion-test arch response
Tibia (rotated)HVLAExt-rotated tibia: internally rotate, flex knee to barrier, short J-motion thrust medial-to-lateral. Int-rotated tibia: externally rotate, flex to barrier, thrust lateral-to-medial. Avoid if acute instability/fracture/severe sprain/patient can't relax
Hamstring - lateral (biceps femoris)CounterstrainProne; tender point below ischial tuberosity or ~1/3 above fibular head; mark 10/10; flex knee markedly, externally rotate tibia on femur, fine-tune hip extension/compression until tenderness reduced; hold ~90 sec, slow return
Hamstring - medial (semimembranosus/semitendinosus)CounterstrainProne; flex knee markedly, internally rotate tibia on femur, fine-tune hip extension/compression until tenderness reduced; hold ~90 sec, slow return
Quick reference

Condition one-liners

  • Plantar fasciitis: microtrauma/fibrosis from plantar fascial tension; heel pain + arch/footwear risks.
  • Morton neuroma: interdigital nerve compression, usually 3rd-4th toes; Mulder click, tight shoes.
  • Meralgia: lateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression; sensory-only anterolateral thigh.
  • Labral tear: athletic groin pain with click/clunk; FABER/FADIR, MR arthrogram.
  • GTPS: gluteal tendon/bursa/IT band lateral hip pain; pain side-lying, resisted abduction.
  • SI dysfunction: posterior pelvic pain, broad differential; FABER, Gaenslen, distraction, thigh thrust, compression, sacral thrust.
